div.p: Integrated modular design has been widely adopted as an approach to facilitating the development process of largescale real-time systems. Although this approach can achieve enhanced design reuse and reduced time consumption, it results in a complex task allocation and scheduling problem. All tasks should be integrated into a shared platform according to a proper schedule, such that their deadlines will be met even under the worst case situations. In this paper, we study the allocation and scheduling problem of strictly periodic tasks in multi-core real-time systems. We first propose a necessary and sufficient condition to determine whether a new task is schedulable on a processor without changing the start times of the existing tasks. Then, based on the condition derived previously, we present a task assignment algorithm, which not only provides valid start times and processor allocations for all tasks, but also obtains the minimum number of processors required by the system. Finally, simulation experiments with randomly generated task sets are conducted to show the high efficiency and reliability of the proposed approach.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the rapid development of electrical and computer engineering, integrated modular design has been widely adopted in the development process of real-time systems to manipulate numerous sensors, actuators and controllers while maintaining high quality of safety and reliability [1]. Especially for largescale systems, there is an increasing trend towards implementing multiple functionalities upon a shared computing platform [17]. For example, in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) architectures [27], aerospace applications can be developed independently and assembled together upon standard computing resources with temporal and spatial boundaries. The modularization development of the avionics functionalities reduces the complexity of real-time systems and shortens the time on system building, and the integrated design methodology allows hosting the functionalities on a standard computing module and reduces the weight and power consumption.

Although integrated modular design provides notable benefits to real-time systems, it gives rise to a complex task allocation and scheduling problem. All tasks should be integrated together according to a proper strategy such that their deadlines will be met even under the worst case conditions [25]. Typically, in the systems composed of tasks with strict periods, activities are triggered by the progression of time only, and the time interval between any two successive instances of a task is the same and equal to its period. Once the start time of a strictly periodic task is set, the time units occupied by the task's instances are fixed. Thus, the system designers have to provide a proper resource allocation for each task, such that all tasks allocated to the same processor subject to nonoverlapping constraints: no two tasks' instances can overlap during any time period [23].

With the significantly increasing number of tasks, system designers gradually tend to rely on decision-making tools to determine whether all tasks are schedulable upon a multicore platform and to provide valid processor and start time allocations if the tasks are schedulable. Meanwhile, in order to furthest reduce the weight and the power costs, the designers want to find the minimum number of processors on which all tasks can be executed correctly. Therefore, it is necessary and significant to develop a method to allocate the tasks and find the minimum number of processors required by all tasks.
In this paper, we study the allocation and scheduling problem of tasks with strict periods in multi-core real-time systems. We aim to address two aspects appearing in the system design:

1. How to determine whether a strictly periodic task is schedulable in a multi-core system? 2. How many processors are at least required such that all strictly periodic tasks in a real-time system can run without any collision?

To the best of our knowledge, there are two types of solutions focusing on the first aspect. The first type extends the schedulability analysis of two tasks to a multi-task situation with restrictions that narrow the range of application. In [16], the authors gave a schedulability condition when the greatest common divisor of the periods of each two tasks was the same. In [22], a schedulability determination was derived under the constraint that the period of new task was a multiple of one of the periods of the existing tasks. The second type of solutions is based on the critical scaling factor [20] (i.e., the largest possible change for all task execution times). In [1] and [24], the authors calculated the critical scaling factor by a bestresponse algorithm, and used the value calculated to determine whether all tasks can be allocated to a limited number of processors.

Very little research has been carried out into the second aspect because of its considerable complexity. In [9], the authors obtained the minimum number of the processors required by a task set under the condition that the periods of all tasks were harmonic, i.e., for any two tasks, the period of one task is a multiple of that of the other one. However, this strict constraint prohibits the widespread use of these results.

div.head: A. Contributions
div.p: This research studies the schedulability conditions for tasks with strict periods and presents a heuristic to solve the processor and start time allocation problem in a multi-core real-time system. The main results and contributions in this paper are as follows.

First, we derive a sufficient and necessary condition to determine whether a new task is schedulable on a given processor without changing the start times of all existing tasks. This condition helps the system designers in selecting a proper processor to each task. Meanwhile, this condition is able to work in multi-task situations, and does not require any iteration. Hence, it is effective and has a relatively wide range of applications.

Second, with the schedulability condition derived, we present a task assignment algorithm to allocate a valid processor and start time for each task and get an upper bound on the number of processors required by the tasks. Even though this algorithm is not optimal and the number obtained is not the minimum one, it provides a guarantee that all tasks can be scheduled correctly upon a platform if the number of processors is not less than the value calculated from this algorithm.

The proposed approach has a wide range of applications and can be adapted to tasks with both harmonic and nonharmonic periods in a multi-core real-time system. We compare the approach with the other similar solutions and evaluate its performance on time consumption, acceptance ratios and relative error ratios.

div.head: B. Organization
div.p: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the related work. Section III gives the basic notations and the model used for strictly periodic tasks. Section IV analyzes the schedulability of strictly periodic tasks through several theorems, and proposes a schedulability condition when all existing tasks keep fixed. Section V introduces an approach to distribute all tasks to the processors and get the number of cores required. Section VI uses simulation experiments to evaluate the performance of our approach. Finally, Sect. VII gives a summary of this paper and the directions for future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In the field of real-time scheduling, there have been many works studying the allocation and scheduling of periodic tasks. In Ramamritham [25], the author discussed a static algorithm to determine the allocation and start times of subtasks of complex periodic tasks. The proposed algorithm handled precedence, communication and fault tolerance requirements as well as the periodicity constraints that had been considered in Bannister and Trivedi [2] and Sha et al. [26]. Baruah and Chakraborty [3] analyzed the schedulability of the nonpreemptive recurring task model and proposed a condition for uniprocessor scheduling. Chwa [6] studied the fully-migrative scheduling problem of tasks on heterogeneous multicore platforms, and Lee [19] developed a divide-and-conquer technique and adopted the notion of time-reversibility for tighter schedulability guarantees. However, in all of those works, the periods of tasks were not strict and some slack time was allowed between successive instances of a periodic task.

The allocation and scheduling of strictly periodic tasks is classified as a non-preemptive and strictly periodic multiprocessor scheduling problem [1]. This problem is very challenging, not only because the non-preemption property gives it a NP-Hard computational complexity [14], but also because the strict periodicity makes it more difficult to derive the schedulability conditions. Korst et al. [18] discussed the computational complexity of the periodic scheduling problems and gave a sufficient and necessary schedulability condition for two tasks, which had been proven to be a sufficient condition [16] in multi-task situations. Kermia et al. [15] presented a greedy algorithm to solve the allocation and scheduling problem with precedence and periodicity constraints considered in Cucu and Sorel [7]. Eisenbrand et al. [9] proposed a schedulability condition and distributed tasks on a minimum number of identical machines under the constraint that the periods of all tasks were harmonic. Marouf and Sorel [22] did a similar work and derived a local schedulability condition for non-harmonic tasks when the period of a new task was a multiple of one of the periods of the existing tasks.

The allocation and scheduling problem of strictly periodic tasks on a multi-core platform has also received considerable attentions in current years. For example, Al-Sheikh et al. [1] first used the Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) formulation to build an exact framework for the scheduling problem in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) platform where all avionic tasks are real-time and under strict periodicity constraint. Then, they presented a best response algorithm based on the game theoretic approach [11] to calculate the largest possible change for the execution times of all tasks. Finally, the authors used the common scaling factor to determine whether or not all strictly periodic tasks were schedulable upon a limited number of processors. Based on the work of Al-Sheikh et al., Pira and Artigues [24] presented a new method to compute the best response and improved the original algorithm with local optimizations and a propagation mechanism.

In Chen et al. [5], the authors represented a strictly periodic task by its eigentask, computed all valid scheduling slots for the eigentask and proposed a condition to determine whether a task is schedulable on a given processor. The schedulability condition proposed is just a sufficient condition and only works when the start times of all existing tasks are fixed. In this research, we also adopt the idea of eigentask; however, we use a more efficient method to calculate the valid scheduling slots of an eigentask. We not only provide a necessary and sufficient schedulability condition, but also present an approach to allocate the tasks and obtain the number of processors required. The approach proposed in this paper has a wider application range and a higher scheduling success ratio.

div.head: III. NOTATIONS AND SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this work, we deal with a real-time system consisting of m identical cores on which a set of n tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } to be allocated and scheduled. Each task is independent and with strict periodicity constraint. A task is characterized by a triple τ i = c i , p i , s i where p i is its period, c i is the worst case execution time (WCET), and s i is its offset (i.e., the start time of its first instance) with 0 ≤ s i ≤ p ic i . When the offset of τ i is unknown, we use a tuple τ i = c i , p i to denote the task τ i . We assume that the tasks' timing parameters (i.e., p i , c i and s i ) are all integers. Figure 1 describes an example of a strictly periodic task used in this paper. A task τ i generates one instance with the worst case execution time c i at every time unit s i + kp i . Each instance needs to be executed immediately after its generation and finished before the beginning of s i + kp i + c i without any other tasks' interrupt, which can be characterized by an open interval [s i + kp i , s i + kp i + c i ). We use B k i (s i ) to characterize the time units occupied by the kth instance of τ i , then there is:
div.formula: τ i ∈ T, ∀k ≥ 0, B k i (s i ) = [s i + kp i , s i + kp i + c i )
div.p: . Let E i denote the time units used by all instances of a task τ i , i.e., E i = k∈N B k i (s i ). In this work, tasks are not equally allocated to the m processors, and then the number of tasks hosted by each processor may be different. We use T p and n p to denote all tasks and the number of tasks allocated to a processor p (1 ≤ p ≤ m). Let mc represent the minimum number of processors required by a task set T . Then, m ≥ mc means all tasks in T can be allocated and scheduled upon an m-core platform; otherwise, mcm more cores are needed. Now we introduce two more notations which will be used in the following sections. We use P max to denote the largest period of all tasks in the T , and use g i,j to represent the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the periods of any two tasks τ i and τ j , i.e., P max def = max 1≤i≤n p i , g i,j = GCD(p i , p j ). div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR TASKS WITH STRICT PERIODS
div.p: In the section, we discuss how to determine whether a new task is schedulable on a given processor when the offsets of all existing tasks keep fixed. We first introduce a schedulability condition for two tasks running on the same processor. Then we represent a task by its eigentask, whose WCET is 1 and period is the same as that of the original task. Finally, we calculate all free time units that the eigentask can use, and determine whether there are sufficiently many (i.e., as many as the original task's WCET) consecutive free time units available. If there are, the original task is determined schedulable. When two tasks τ i and τ j are allocated to the same processor, they are schedulable if and only if there is no overlapping time unit among their instances. It can be expressed as: τ i and τ j are schedulable on the same processor if and only if
div.formula: ∀k, l ≥ 0, B k i (s i ) ∩ B l j (s j ) = ∅.(1)
div.p: Although Eq. ( 1) is a necessary and sufficient condition, it could not be applied directly in solving the schedulability problem of two tasks. This is because Eq. ( 1) needs to calculate the time intervals occupied by all instances of the tasks. However, the instances of a strictly periodic task will be regenerated in every cycle and their number is infinite. The following theorem was first proposed by Korst [18] and gives a more efficient schedulability condition.
Theorem 1. Two tasks τ i = c i , p i , s i and τ j = c j , p j , s j are schedulable on the same processor if and only if
div.formula: c i ≤ (s j -s i )mod(g i,j ) ≤ g i,j -c j (2)
div.p: Theorem 1 provides a schedulability condition for two tasks and does not require computing the time units used by all instances of the tasks. However, it cannot work in the situation that contains more than two tasks. It is quite difficult to give a determination of whether a new task is schedulable with all existing tasks in a multi-task set. We solve this problem by applying the notion of eigentask, which was first presented by Chen et al. [5] and inspired from the idea of eigenvector [12] in the matrix theory.

div.head: B. Eigentask
div.p: Assume that all tasks in a set T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } are already schedulable, and a new task τ r = c r , p r is to be scheduled. If we can get all valid free time units for the task τ r = 1, p r , it is easy to determine whether sufficiently many consecutive slots are available for τ r . If there are, the original task τ r can be scheduled with all tasks in T .

We refer to τ r = 1, p r as the eigentask of the original task τ r = c r , p r . Then, tasks with the same periods have the same eigentask. In the following, we calculate all valid free time units for the eigentask of a new task with a modular arithmetic method.

We take a modulo operation on the time units occupied by all instances of an existing task with the period of an eigentask. We refer to the results of the modulo operation as modular busy time units. Then, for each time unit that the existing tasks run on, there is an associated modular busy time unit coerced into a reference period. For example, if e is a time unit used by a task τ i , e = e mod p r is the corresponding modular busy time unit according to the modulo operation on the period p r . Example 1 describes the modulo operation and shows the relationship between time units used and the modular busy time units. We use BT U (i, r) to denote the modular busy time units of τ i according to the modulo operation on the period of τ r , then:

div.p: With the modular busy time units, we present a necessary and sufficient schedulability condition for any task τ i and an eigentask τ r .

div.head: C. Schedulability Determination
div.p: In this section, we give a theorem to determine whether a new task can be added into a multi-core system without changing the offsets of the existing tasks. We need to introduce two symbols LLC and SLC, which were first used in [?]. Let S be a non-empty set of integers, LLC(S) represents the largest length of consecutive integers in S, and SLC(S, l) denotes a set constituted of integers from which l consecutive integers are all in S, i.e., SLC(S, l) = {x | x + y ∈ S, ∀y ∈ [0, l)}. For example, an integer set S = {1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10}, the maximum length of consecutive integers in S is 4, i.e., LLC(S) = 4. If the given consecutive length is 3, the subset meets the requirement is {7, 8}, i.e., SLC(S, 3) = {7, 8}.

Theorem 4 shows that, when all existing tasks keep fixed, a new task is schedulable if and only if its worst case execution time is not larger than the maximum length of consecutive free time units of its eigentask. With this theorem, we propose a first-fit algorithm to allocate the tasks and obtain the minimum number of processors required by all tasks in the following section.

V. TASK ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM Theorem 4 derived in Sect. IV-C provides a determination of whether a new task can be added into a multi-core realtime system. It helps the designers in producing a proper scheduling table such that all tasks can be executed without any overlapping unit. In this section, we propose a first-fit algorithm to allocate the tasks to the processors one by one and calculate the number of processors required by all tasks. If the task currently considered is determined schedulable according to Condition (8), it will be allocated to the first processor that can execute it correctly; otherwise, a new idle processor is required. When all tasks have been considered, the number of cores required by the tasks is acquired. In the following, we describe the algorithm in Sect. V-A, show its limitations in Sect. V-B and analyze its running time cost in Sect. V-C.

div.head: A. Task Assignment Algorithm
div.p: In this section, we present a task assignment algorithm which not only produces a valid processor and start time allocations for the tasks, but also provides an upper bound on the number of processors required by all tasks.

For each task τ i (1 ≤ i ≤ n), our task assignment algorithm uses Condition (8) to determine whether τ i can be allocated to the processor j (at first j = 0). There are two cases depending on whether τ i is schedulable on the processor j.
(A) If yes. Use Condition (9) to get the start time for τ i , add τ i into T j , and increase the number of tasks on the processor j by 1.

(B) If no. τ i cannot be allocated to the processor j. Determine whether τ i can be schedulable on the processor j + 1. If j is the last processor considered currently, a new idle processor is required now. Then allocate τ i to the new processor, assign 0 to the start time of τ i , and increase the number of processors used by 1.

The task assignment algorithm stops after all tasks in the set T have been allocated. mc represents the number of cores required by the tasks and T p (1 ≤ p ≤ mc) denotes the set of tasks allocated to the processor p with assigned offset for each task. If mc ≤ m, all tasks in T can be allocated and scheduled on this multi-core platform; otherwise mcm more cores are required. The pseudo-code for this task assignment algorithm is given in Algorithm 1.

div.head: B. Limitation Analysis
div.p: Even though this task assignment algorithm can determine whether all tasks are schedulable upon a limited number of processors and provide a proper offset and processor allocation for each task, it is not an optimal method and the number of processors calculated by this algorithm is not the minimum one. For each task, this task assignment algorithm selects the first processor on which sufficiently many consecutive free time units are available, and chooses one of the integers from its valid offsets. Actually, in a multi-core real-time system, there could be many processors and offsets which guarantee the task runs without any overlapping units. This algorithm provides one of possible task allocations, and the number of processors acquired from this algorithm is an upper bound of the minimum one. It just provides a guarantee that all tasks can be allocated and scheduled correctly upon a platform if the number of processors is not less than the value calculated from this algorithm.

div.head: C. Running Time Analysis
div.p: We analyze the computational complexity of the task assignment algorithm proposed in this section. From Algorithm 1 we know, the main computation part of the algorithm is from line 2 to 21, which has a structure of double closed loops. We consider the inner loop (from line 4 to 14) first. The inner loop stops when τ i can be allocated to one of the processors. In the worst case, all tasks are used to calculate the free time units of the eigentask of τ i . Then the largest running time cost of the inner loop is O (np i ), where n is the number of tasks in the system. We use P max to denote the largest period of all tasks, then the inner loop runs in O (nP max ). Now we analyze the running time cost of the outer loop which repeats n times. Each time the algorithm uses the inner loop to determine whether the task currently considered is schedulable on one of the processors. Lines from 15 to 20 allocate the task to a new processor, and runs in O (1). Then the overall time cost of each outer loop is O (nP max )+O (1), which is equal to O (nP max ). Given the outer loops repeats n times, the total running time of Algorithm 1 is O (n 2 P max ).

Since the running time cost of Algorithm 1 depends on the number of tasks n and the largest period P max of all tasks, this task assignment algorithm runs in pseudo-polynomial time. The complexity explodes as soon as n becomes large. However, the number of calculation steps of this algorithm is considered in a very pessimistic situation, we find in our experiments that average performances typically performs better to solve the allocation and scheduling problems.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we conduct experiments to evaluate the performance of the task assignment algorithm proposed. We compare our approach with two existing solutions including the exact method Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) [21] and the task assignment algorithm based on eigentask and mapping function (EMTA) proposed in [5]. The experiments were performed on an Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-3320M CPU 2.60GHz with 4.00GB of system memory.

div.head: A. Task Generation
div.p: We generate our tasks with the UUnifast-Discard algorithm [8], which is a simple extension of UUniFast [4] in multicore situations and produces a random utilization for each task under a given system utilization. There were three parameters used in the task generation process: the number of tasks n, the system utilization u and the task type (harmonic or nonharmonic).

The generation procedure was the same as that described in [5]. First we adopted UUnifast-Discard algorithm to generate the random utilization u i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) for each task, i.e., u = 1≤i≤n u i . Then, an integer value p 0 from 5 to 9 was chosen uniformly as a base value, i.e., p 1 = U [5,9]. Subsequently, for non-harmonic tasks, periods were chosen randomly from the set {2 x 3 y 5 z p 0 : x, y, z ∈ [0, 4]}, which inspired from [10]. For harmonic tasks, p 0 was the period of the first task and a period ratio k i (1 < i ≤ n) was selected randomly from [1,6]. The periods of the harmonic tasks were constructed as p i = k i p i-1 . Finally, the worst case execution time of each task was constructed as c i = p i u i .
In the following, we evaluate the performance of the solutions in terms of execution time in Sect. VI-B, acceptance ratio in Sect. VI-C and deviation ratio in Sect. VI-D.

VI) represents the average value of the experimental results of 100 instances.

As can be seen in Fig. 3, the time consumption of three solutions grows gradually along with increase of the number of tasks, no matter they are chosen from harmonic or nonharmonic periods. The reason is that with a larger number of tasks, more processor and start time allocations need to be considered by the solutions. We can also find that when the number of tasks is more than 5, the time consumption of our approach is less than those of other solutions. This is because our approach considers tasks one by one and does not require any iteration. When the number of tasks chosen from harmonic periods is 25, the time consumption of our approach is 7.9 seconds, which is 1.9 times and 74 times less than those of EMTA method and MILP respectively.

In the experiment of Fig. 4, the speed of our approach is evaluated by varying the system utilizations. As expected, the time consumption becomes higher when more tasks are tested on. Meanwhile, when the number of tasks is fixed, the execution time of our approach grows along with the increase of the system utilizations. This is because that a larger system utilization means tasks with larger worst case execution times were generated, and more operations are required to calculate Fig. 4. Time consumption of our approach on harmonic tasks generated with different system utilizations the free time units used for a new task. Then larger system utilization means more time is required when the number of tasks is fixed.

div.head: C. Acceptance Ratio Evaluation
div.p: In this section, we compare the performances of MILP formulation, EMTA method and our approach in terms of acceptance ratio [13], i.e., the percentage of task sets determined schedulable on a limited number of processors. Some task sets that are rejected by one solution, can be determined schedulable by other solutions. We perform the experiments on the same task sets, and record the number of task sets that are successfully scheduled by each solution. A higher acceptance ratio indicates a more accurate and useful method, since all solutions are tested on the same task sets. Fig. 5. Acceptance ratios of solutions on non-harmonic tasks when the system utilization is 1.0

In the experiment of Fig. 5, tasks are generated with non-harmonic periods when the system utilization is 1.0. The number of processors in the system is limited to 8. It demonstrates that the acceptance ratios of the three solutions have a similar changing tendency that they gradually decrease from 100 percent to less than 60 percent along with increase of the number of tasks. MILP which is an exact method, has the highest acceptance ratio on a given number of tasks. Our approach performs a better performance in terms of acceptance ratio than EMTA method. This is because that schedulability condition used in our approach is necessary and sufficient, while in EMTA method a sufficient condition is adopted. In the experiment of Fig. 6, ten tasks are chosen from nonharmonic periods, and we evaluate the acceptance ratios of the three solutions by tuning the system utilization from 0.05 to 0.4. The number of processors is limited to 2. The acceptance ratios of all three solution decrease along with the increase of the system utilizations. As expected, our approach still has the second highest performance under the same system utilization.

div.head: D. Deviation Ratio Evaluation
div.p: At last, we evaluate the performance of our approach by comparing the numbers of required processors found by the solutions. MILP formulation can find the minimum number of processors required by a task set because it is an exact method and can completely search the solution space. We show the results from two aspects: average number and deviation ratio [5]. Average number represents the average value of the numbers of required processors found by a solution. A smaller average number means a more accurate method since all solutions are tested on the same task sets. Deviation ratio dr, is the relative error ratio between the number of required processors found by a non-exact method and the minimum number, i.e., dr = (N EW -M ILP )/M ILP × 100%. Deviation ratio is a means to check up on the reliability of the solutions. A solution which has a lower deviation ratio, is more reliable and useful. In the experiment of Fig. 7, tasks are generated with nonharmonic periods when the system utilization is 1.0. We can find that more processors are required when the number of tasks grows. As expected, MILP can use the least number of processors to allocate and schedule the tasks. Our approach has the second best performance and the difference between MILP and our approach is slight. When the number of tasks is 25, the largest difference appears and its value is 0.95. However, at the same time, the difference between MILP and EMTA method is 1.7, which is 1.79 times as much as that between MILP and our approach. Through varying the system utilizations, the deviation ratio of our approach is evaluated in Fig. 8. The tasks are chosen from non-harmonic periods. As can be seen that all deviation ratios grow with the number of tasks. However, when the number of tasks is fixed, the deviation ratio of our approach becomes higher along with the system utilization increases. The reason is that with a larger system utilization, larger worst case execution time is generated and more cores are required. More and more valid offset and assignment allocations for tasks need to be considered. However, our approach dose not search all the solution space, and the differences between the numbers of processors found by MILP and our approach become larger. Then, a larger system utilization leads to a higher deviation ratio.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS AND FURTHER WORK
div.p: In this paper, we aim at providing a valid start time and processor allocations for the strictly periodic tasks. Through the multi-task schedulability analysis, we proposed a condition to determine whether a task was schedulable without modifying the existing tasks. Then, with this schedulability conditions, we presented a task assignment algorithm to allocate the tasks and calculate the number of cores required. Even the number obtained by our approach is not the minimum one; it gives an upper bound of the minimum number.

Although our approach can obtain a reasonable solution in a relatively short amount of time, we would like to find a more efficient way to reduce the search space and improve its performance. Meanwhile, we are interested in studying the scheduling problem of strict periodic tasks in conjunction with non-strictly ones upon a multi-core platform, and would like to see whether some of the results proposed here can be extended to the non-strictly periodic scheduling.
